hook_text: In about 5 billion years, the Sun will swell up and swallow Mercury and Venus. Here's how stars die.
clip_script: When a star like the Sun runs out of hydrogen in its centre, gravity squeezes the core and the outside puffs up, cools and turns red. It becomes a red giant. Our Sun may grow about 200 times wider, swallowing Mercury and Venus and scorching the Earth. Then it gently blows its outer layers into space as a glowing shell called a planetary nebula, which has nothing to do with planets. What's left is a white dwarf: the size of the Earth, so dense that a teaspoon would weigh several tonnes, slowly cooling for billions of years. Bigger stars go out with a bang, as supernovae. And everything they throw out builds new stars, planets and even you.
visual_style: The Sun swelling red over a scorched Earth; the James Webb image of the Southern Ring Nebula; a tiny white dwarf glowing in the centre; a supernova flash scattering glowing elements.
pacing: Shock open, a slow swelling, a gentle exhale into the nebula, an explosive contrast, a personal star-stuff close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and trace the elements in your body back to the stars.
